title: Define canonical city data model v0 (core schema + optional enrichments + mapping rules)
description: From the city survey, define the canonical model the engine targets: (1) core expenditures schema — the fields most cities publish (payee, agency/department, amount, dates, fiscal year, category, fund) with required-vs-optional tiers; (2) optional enrichment tables (salaries, capital projects, contractor licenses) that light up features when present; (3) mapping-rule format for source->canonical column translation, incl. multi-era schema breaks; (4) how canonicalization (agency/payee normalization) and data-quality flags (offsetting, artifacts) generalize per city. Deliverable: docs/canonical-model.md + the schema portion of the city config format. Louisville must be expressible in this model with zero information loss (current DATA_DICTIONARY maps cleanly onto it).
close_reason: docs/canonical-model.md: tiered core expenditures schema (required/recommended/optional + extension-column rule guaranteeing zero loss), 6 optional enrichment tables incl. new budget table, era-based source mapping rules with YAML config shapes, canonicalization + data-quality flags generalized. Louisville verified 24/24 columns zero-loss; Cincinnati/KC/Baltimore/Chicago fits checked against surveyed schemas. Acceptance for the refactor (jy0) spelled out.

title: Survey open data portals of ~10 target cities (schemas, formats, metadata quality)
description: For a sample of cities on ArcGIS Hub (plus 1-2 Socrata cities for contrast — e.g. Lexington, Nashville, Cincinnati, Indianapolis, Kansas City, Tucson, Chattanooga, Durham, plus Chicago/Baltimore on Socrata): catalog which Lou-relevant datasets each publishes (expenditures/checkbook, salaries, capital projects, contractor licenses, demographics), and for each record: schema fields, API access pattern, update cadence, historical depth, schema breaks across years (like Louisville's 2008-2017 vs 2018+ split), and metadata quality (are columns documented at all?). Deliverable: docs/city-survey.md comparison matrix + a shortlist of best second-city candidates. This grounds the canonical schema in what cities actually publish instead of guessing from Louisville alone.
close_reason: Survey complete: 11 cities + Louisville baseline in docs/city-survey.md with comparison matrix, shortlist (Cincinnati 5/5, Kansas City 5/5, Baltimore 3/5 zero-plumbing, Chicago 4/5), and six canonical-model implications feeding louisville-open-data-8ve. Headline: only 6 of 12 cities have a live checkbook; both top candidates are Socrata; per-year fragmentation + schema breaks are the norm; metadata is universally undocumented (the curation IS the product).

title: Universal city data model: works for most cities with open data
description: Adapt Lou's data model from Louisville-specific to a canonical model that fits most cities with open data portals (primarily ArcGIS Hub, the stack most cities share; Socrata for contrast). Approach: survey what target cities actually publish -> derive a canonical schema (core expenditures + optional enrichments) -> refactor the engine to be config-driven (louisville-open-data-jy0) -> prove it by onboarding a second city end-to-end. Success criterion: a new city onboards with a config pack and curation only, no engine changes, and the onboarding effort is measured so we know the real cost of sale. Child of louisville-open-data-ahg.

title: Runtime LLM model fallback so provider deprecations don't require a redeploy
description: Cerebras deprecates models without notice (qwen-3-235b 404 incident; cached answers masked it). Today MODEL is a container env var, so a deprecation means recreating the container. Fix in analytics_agent.py: on 404 model_not_found, fetch /v1/models, pick the first available model from an ordered preference list, log loudly, and surface the active model + any fallback event on /api/health. Current account models (checked 2026-07-30): zai-glm-4.7, gpt-oss-120b (active), gemma-4-31b. This makes the provider question less urgent: Cerebras stays fine for speed/cost once deprecation is survivable.

title: Split data_model.py into generic engine + Louisville city-config pack
description: Everything city-specific is hardcoded in Python today: OLD_TO_NEW schema map, ALL_LABELS, DATA_DICTIONARY, eExpenditures_YYYY.csv filename/era conventions, enrichment table list, agency_mapping.py/payee_mapping.py, and the 8 summary-table SQL blocks (incl. Louisville-specific grant fund LIKE patterns). Goal: a city onboards by writing a config pack (datasets + sources, schema mappings, dictionary/labels, canonicalization maps, summary specs, starter questions) with zero engine changes. Generic pieces already clean: infer_chart, schema description generators, humanize_text, data-quality flag framework. First step: design the config format (YAML/JSON) and prove it by porting Louisville onto it with identical health-endpoint table counts and a passing known-answer suite.
close_reason: data_model.py is now a generic engine; all Louisville specifics live in cities/louisville/ (city.yaml + canonical map CSVs, machine-generated from the old Python structures for fidelity). city_config.py loads packs via CITY_CONFIG env var. Verified identical output: all 17 table counts match pre-refactor baseline exactly (expenditures 2,257,399), 28/28 known-answer tests pass. Paper configs for Cincinnati and Kansas City prove the format on Socrata schemas — both canonical-model acceptance criteria met. Remaining for real second-city onboarding (ftq): socrata reader + fiscal_year derive rule.

title: Lou for cities: productize the civic analytics engine
description: Turn the Louisville-specific bot into a reusable product for any city on an ArcGIS Hub open data portal. See docs/VISION.md. Target customers: municipal governments / Esri partner ecosystem. Children: engine/config refactor, model resilience, RAG over city documents, uptime monitoring.

title: Prove portability: onboard a second city end-to-end with a config pack
description: Pick the best candidate from the city survey shortlist and stand it up on the config-driven engine: write its config pack (datasets, schema mappings, dictionary, canonicalization seeds, summary specs, starter questions), pull its data, and get the bot answering real questions about that city. Measure and record the actual onboarding effort (hours, and which steps were curation vs config vs code) — that number is the cost-of-sale input for the Lou-for-cities pitch and the proof the canonical model works beyond Louisville. Any engine change required to make the second city work is a bug in the canonical model/refactor to feed back upstream.

title: Uptime monitoring for louisville.raylytics.io
description: Prod verified healthy 2026-07-30 (health OK, /api/ask returns 200 SSE through Cloudflare), but nothing watches it. Add a scheduled end-to-end probe: GET /api/health AND the empty-question POST /api/ask SSE probe (the free no-LLM check from CLAUDE.md), alerting on failure. Options: cron/launchd on mac-server, or a free external uptime service hitting both endpoints. Must catch the model-deprecation failure mode: health can be ok while live LLM calls 404, so also alert when errors_last_hour on /api/health is nonzero.

title: RAG spike: ground answers in city documents (press releases, budget books, council minutes)
description: SQL answers the 'what'; documents answer the 'why' (e.g. a 2021 spend spike is ARPA — that context lives in press releases and budget narratives, not the ledger). Spike scope: (1) ingest a small corpus — Louisville Metro press releases, budget book PDFs, council meeting minutes; (2) chunk + embed into DuckDB VSS (keeps the single-engine story) or sqlite-vec; (3) add a retrieval step that feeds top-k chunks into the interpretation phase with source citations in the SSE answer; (4) decide routing: always-retrieve vs a router that classifies data-vs-context questions. Deliverable: design note + working prototype on one document type before generalizing. This is also a product differentiator per docs/VISION.md — metadata/context quality is the bottleneck cities can't solve themselves.
